title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
materials: Woodblock print; ink and color on paper
official_description: Hokusai's woodblock print sets an enormous curling wave and three boats against a distant Mount Fuji.
historical_context: Published around 1830-1832 as part of Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, the print used newly available Prussian blue.
visual_description: A claw-like wave arches over three narrow boats while foam scatters like fingers and snow-capped Mount Fuji appears small in the distance.

chunks.text: Katsushika Hokusai designed Under the Wave off Kanagawa, commonly called The Great Wave, around 1830-1832 in Edo-period Japan.
The print belongs to Hokusai's landscape series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which repeatedly presents Japan's sacred mountain from changing places and conditions.
It is a color woodblock print made with ink and color on paper, not a unique oil painting.
The Metropolitan Museum impression numbered JP1847 measures 25.7 by 37.9 centimetres.
An enormous curling wave rises above three long boats, while white foam forms pointed, claw-like shapes around the crest.
Mount Fuji appears very small inside the hollow beneath the wave, making the near water seem even larger and more dangerous.
Hokusai uses a dramatic contrast of scale and distance: the nearby wave dominates, the boats are trapped beneath it, and Mount Fuji recedes toward the horizon.
The design was among the early Japanese prints to feature imported Prussian blue, a vivid synthetic pigment that resisted fading better than older blue dyes.
Many impressions were printed from the same carved blocks. They vary because blocks wore down and printers changed color and registration during production.
Woodblock prints were affordable popular objects rather than single luxury paintings, helping this dramatic design circulate widely.
The tiny people and boats face nature's beauty and danger, while distant Mount Fuji appears calm and enduring.
Hokusai made a print of a giant blue wave curling over three little boats. Far away, Mount Fuji looks tiny but steady.
The publisher advertised the Fuji series around New Year 1831 using Prussian blue as a selling point; technical analysis links the color to a double woodblock printing process.
There is no single definitive physical Great Wave: surviving impressions show differences in line breaks, pigment, wear, and printing sequence while sharing Hokusai's design.
Hokusai designed the image, then specialists transferred the design, carved blocks, and printed the colors. The publisher financed and distributed the prints.
Despite its title, the series eventually contained forty-six prints: its success led the publisher to add ten views to the original thirty-six.
Katsushika Hokusai a cree Sous la vague au large de Kanagawa, appelee La Grande Vague, vers 1830-1832 pendant l'epoque d'Edo.
L'estampe appartient a la serie Trente-six vues du mont Fuji, qui montre la montagne sacree depuis differents lieux.
Il s'agit d'une estampe sur bois imprimee avec de l'encre et des couleurs sur papier, et non d'une peinture unique.
Une vague immense se courbe au-dessus de trois bateaux. Son ecume blanche forme des pointes semblables a des griffes.
Le mont Fuji parait minuscule dans le creux de la vague, ce qui agrandit encore la menace de l'eau au premier plan.
L'oeuvre fait partie des premieres estampes japonaises utilisant le bleu de Prusse, un pigment synthetique vif qui resistait mieux a la decoloration.
De nombreuses impressions ont ete tirees des memes blocs. L'usure du bois et les choix des imprimeurs expliquent leurs petites differences.
Les petits humains affrontent la beaute et le danger de la nature, tandis que le mont Fuji reste calme au loin.
Hokusai a dessine le motif, puis des specialistes ont transfere le dessin, grave les blocs et imprime les couleurs. L'editeur financait et diffusait les estampes.
Malgre son titre, la serie compte finalement quarante-six estampes: son succes a conduit l'editeur a ajouter dix vues aux trente-six premieres.
